cells.tense: What you have tended is bearing fruit, and you are standing in it with the pen in hand.
cells.act: let the friction test what you are committed to
cells.ask: Go at the awkward part of a commitment you already carry. Stay in that friction longer than is comfortable, then notice what held.
cells.core:
What you have tended is bearing fruit. You can enjoy it without totting it up, because you were there for all the parts nobody applauded, and you know what they were worth. Under weight you keep your shape without going stiff, and that is what carried the thing this far.

Take a commitment you already carry and walk into the awkward part you keep putting off. Stay in that friction longer than is comfortable, then look at what held. You are not checking whether you still want it — you are checking what it is made of. Some of the work ahead is upkeep, not arrival. That is the price of something that grew.

cells.verb: growing what careful tending has produced
cells.place: where you hold under weight — the endurance that keeps form without going rigid

cells.tense: You will be gripping the whole harvest before it has finished, braced against a future that can't be written.
cells.act: join someone in the work so the two streams run as one
cells.ask: Bring one person who matters into this week's work so you're carrying it together, at a pace you both agree on.
cells.core:
The yield is close, and you are already hauling what it will need: next season, next request, what could go wrong, all carried at once. Under that load the grip hardens, and the things you tend stay young and unfinished, because something still becoming can't be judged yet and stays yours to hold. From the outside it looks like the garden is being kept from coming in.

Bring one person who matters into this week's work so the two of you carry it together at a pace you both agree on. Two streams running as one. Put down the second and third load, and let what is growing come in on the season it chooses.
cells.sheetLine: You're gripping the harvest before it has finished growing.

cells.tense: There was a garden, and you have been standing at the gate of it since it went in.
cells.act: face one way for three days
cells.ask: For three days, go one direction you actually want — a want, not the sensible choice — and give the other options nothing.
cells.core:
You can carry what has to be carried without making a fuss about the weight, and you have been doing it a long while. The garden is there. You speak about it in the past, as something that happened once, and you are not standing in it now. Nothing has drained out of you — you have just stopped pointing any of it at something you want.

For three days, go one direction you actually want, and let that set the heading rather than the sensible option. Give the other options nothing. It is small enough to do while tired, and once you are facing one way, the loading stops being pure upkeep.
cells.sheetLine: The garden is there and you're standing outside it.

cells.tense: The yield is in and you keep filing it under the season's luck, the pen already in your hand.
cells.act: release the method, not the purpose
cells.ask: Think back to a stretch where something you were committed to stopped working. Notice the method you dropped, then the purpose you kept.
cells.core:
The garden is bearing and you call that good luck or the right year. You remember the parts nobody watched — dropping the method that had gone useless while keeping the purpose intact — and you have shelved all of it as circumstance. It was your hands in the ground. What got made, got made by you, and the account you would give says otherwise.

Think back to a stretch where something you were committed to stopped working. Notice the method you dropped, then the purpose you kept. Because setting down a method that has finished its job is not defeat — it is what let the purpose survive. Seen that way, the work has an author.
cells.sheetLine: The yield isn't the season's luck. It came from your hands.
